evidence_fragments.content:
Robotics: Science and Systems 2024
Delft, Netherlands, July 15-July 19, 2024
World Models for General Surgical Grasping
Hongbin Lin 1, Bin Li 1, Chun Wai Wong 1, Juan Rojas 2, Xiangyu Chu 1, and Kwok Wai Samuel Au 1

We propose a world-model-based deep reinforcement
learning framework “Grasp Anything for Surgery” (GAS), that
learns a pixel-level visuomotor policy for surgical grasping,
enhancing both generality and robustness.

Videos and codes can be found on our project page:
https://linhongbin.github.io/gas/.

Our vi-
suomotor policy, which is trained in simulation and
directly transferred to a real robot without further fine-
tuning, demonstrates high generality with significant per-
formance (average 69% success rate) and extraordinary
robustness against disturbances in the environment.

Compared to their works,
we learned a single visuomotor controller for diverse grasping
tasks.

We aim to actuate an unknown robot
gripper to grasp and lift an unknown target object (10mm to
50mm) lying on a phantom plane via a learned visuomotor
policy π that maps temporal RGB-D images to a discrete
action command.

Discrete commands actuate
the gripper in 2mm increments across Cartesian dimensions
and rotations steps of 10 degrees about the z-axis (normal
to the plane) w.r.t to a world frame. Positive and negative
directions are output independently and are mutually exclusive.
When one direction is activated, the other will be null. The
gripper has an open and closed mode. As such, there are a
total of 9 discrete commands at at each timestep. We set the
horizon H in our grasping tasks to 300 timesteps. The task is
successful if the stuff is grasped and the target object is lifted
10 mm above the plane.

When the gripper’s desired position is outside the workspace,
the actuated position is clipped to the point in the workspace
closest to the desired position.

It consists of 2 components: i) world
models, targeting to learn the POMDP dynamics with on-
policy rollouts from environments, and ii) a control policy,
targeting to optimize by merely simulated rollouts from the
learned world models. Both world models and the control
policy are learned simultaneously. In this paper, our proposed
framework, GAS, is built upon DreamerV2 for visuomotor
learning in a more challenging visual manipulation setting,
surgical grasping. Details of DreamerV2 can be found in [26].

Fig. 3. An overview of Grasp Anything for Surgery (GAS). Visual observations are processed by our proposed video processing, including video object
segmentation, depth estimation, and Dynamic Spotlight Adaptation (DSA). A visuomotor policy, learned by world models, leverages the processed observations
as the input. The predicted action of the policy, further processed by Virtual Clutch (VC), actuates the robot gripper to grasp target objects in simulation and
a real robot. Furthermore, domain randomization is applied in simulation for visuomotor learning.

TAM
combines the Segment-Anything Model (SAM) [41], a large
foundation model for image segmentation, and an advanced
VOS model, XMem [42].

label a fine mask for an object using SAM with only a
few point prompts (around 2 clicks of point prompts for
each object mask). The labeled image-mask pair is saved
for further tracking.
• Online-Tracking Stage : Given the image-mask pair of
annotation in the first frame, object masks for the rest
frames of the streaming RGB-D images are automati-
cally tracked using XMem, which predicts object masks
according to both temporal and spatial correspondence of
historical RGB images.
Using TAM, there is no need to prepare datasets or train mod-
els for segmentation. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that we
can re-use the annotation for an object in the annotation stage
if the objects and scene backgrounds are similar, which largely
reduces the effort for annotation. Although TAM can track
any object with arbitrary texture, in practice we attach color
markers to the gripper (See Table I) to enhance the tracking
robustness in real-world scenes of RAS.

In practice, users need to set bi as a hyper-parameter before

One can distinguish between the
estimation and the ground-truth masks by the maximum pixel
error in the mask region between the captured depth image
from the camera and the ground-truth depth image (from eye
observation or prior geometric models) within the workspace.
In the case of our grasping tasks, the maximum pixel error
is set to 10mm.

Fig. 5. Pipeline of Dynamic Spotlight Adaptation (DSA) for visual representation of world models in general surgical grasping. The visual masks, encoding
matrices of mask ID, and the estimated depth image are the inputs of our visual representation. The global layer (red channel) is obtained by generating square
masks and a zoom-in mask based on visual masks, followed by summing these masks with encoding values. The mask (green channel) and the depth layers
(blue channel) are obtained by zooming in a segmented mask image and a segmented depth image, respectively, which can be obtained by multiplication with
visual masks. We stack three layers into a 3D matrix and downsample it to a 64x64x3 compact image for world model learning. Two scalar signals, i.e. the
task-level state and the gripper toggling state, are encoded into two 6x6 square images, which are used to replace pixels of the downsampled image at the
bottom right corner of the global layer (red channel).

The intuition of VC is that the agent starts to move only
when it observes a sufficient amount of temporal visual
observation. As such, we ensure a sufficient low estimation
error when robots interact with the environment. To this end,
we apply VC to learn visuomotor policy in surgical grasping
(see Fig. 6 for the illustration of VC).

positions of the robot arm unchanged, Hclutch is a non-
negative constant determining the timestep that starts to close
the “clutch”, and at is the action predicted by the learned
policy.

• Successful Termination: When the target object is suc-
cessfully grasped and lifted, a reward of 1 is given and
the task is terminated.
• Failed Termination: When the current timestep reaches
the horizon limit, a reward of −0.1 is given and the task
is terminated.
• Normal Progress: When the task proceeds normally with-
out termination flags, a small reward of −0.001 is given
to speed up the grasping. The task is not terminated in
such a task-level state.
• Abnormal Progress : When any of the following three
abnormalities occur: i) the gripper’s desired pose exceeds
the workspace; ii) the target object slides horizontally
due to external forces from the gripper; or iii) the target
object is not in the zoom-in box of DSA, negative
rewards are provided. Particularly, they are set to −0.01,
−0.01, and −0.005 to discourage the occurrence of these
events, respectively. In this task-level state, the task is not
terminated.

For simulation, the benchmark is developed based on an
open-source simulation platform for surgical robot learning,
SurRoL[5]. 3 types of grasping objects (See Fig. 7b), including
needles, boxes, and rods, occur in the task with equal proba-
bilities. We also scale the shape of grasping objects from 0.75
to 1.5 randomly.

For the real robot, we deploy learned controllers to a
surgical robotic arm, Patient Side Manipulator (PSM), in da
Vinci Surgical System controlled by an open-source control
system, da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) [45]. Observed RGB-
D images are captured by an Intel RealSense D435 camera.
A filling light is used to control the illumination condition.

A flag signal, indicating
successful grasping, is manually sent by a joystick based on
human observation. Our FSM transit to the FSM’s state of
successful termination when the grasping flag is sent and
the height of the gripper’s desired pose is above 10mm. We
evaluate controllers on two phantoms, a rectangle phantom,
and a liver phantom (See Fig. 7c-d).

• GAS-RawVR: We replace our visual representation with
RawVR. Scalar signals are encoded to 6x6 square images,
replacing the image pixels in the 1st channel, similar to
our visual representation.

Controllers are trained in the simulation benchmark. In
the training process, controllers are trained with 1.8 million
timesteps; 50 evaluation rollouts are carried out every 200K
training timestep; we pre-fill 10K timesteps of rollouts before
training, including 3K timesteps using a scripted demonstra-
tion policy (approximately 20 rollouts) and 7K timesteps with
a random policy. Each controller is trained with 3 seeds.
We train on 5 computers with 8G-RAM or above GPUs,
where the minimum computer configuration is a laptop with
a 12G-RAM GPU, RTX 4070, and an 8-core CPU. Each
simulation experiment consumes 2-3 days for training. We
select the controller with the highest evaluation score among
the 3 seeds to deploy on the real robot.

In the real robot, the
evaluated controllers run at around 2 Hz, where the computer
configuration is a desktop with a 24G-RAM GPU, Nvidia
TITAN RTX, and an 8-core CPU.

To quantify
the generality, we evaluate 5 unseen target objects and an
unseen gripper as shown in Fig. 2. 20 episodes are evaluated
for each unseen object. For the unseen gripper, we choose the
standard 40mm needle as the target grasping object.

Yet we believe the performance of the baseline
SOTA methods will start to improve if more training steps are
given. The convergence performance of the baseline methods
will be studied in the future.

two types of synthetic noises, image noise
and action noise, are generated by our domain randomization
and added to the observed RGB-D images and desired gripper
pose, respectively; for target disturbance, we use an automatic
rotating platform to move the ground plane with intermittent
and back-and-forth movements so to simulate the target move-
ments placing on the patient’s tissues in real surgery; in the
re-grasping experiments, we manually hit the grasped needle
when the first successful grasp occurs, the target object was
dropped to the plane with a random pose due to the hitting
and the task is successful when the gripper grasp and lift the
target object for the second time within the time limit.

we also observe that our controller does not suffer from the
decrease in success rate caused by the other 5 types of distur-
bance, maintaining success rates above 75%.

Yet, we consider the limitations of our method as follows:
i) failure cases occur due to the reason that the target object
is out of the workspace after the gripper’s horizontal pushing;
ii) the movement speed of the control gripper is limited by a
small incremental action step when using the discrete action
space; iii) the identification of the FSM’s states is based on
human observation and control.

legacy_cells.S: Can a world-model-based visuomotor policy grasp and lift diverse, initially unknown surgical objects with a robot gripper, including under disturbances?

legacy_cells.AK: Segment Anything Model (SAM), used within Track Anything Model for video object segmentation
legacy_cells.AM: Dynamic Spotlight Adaptation stacks global, mask, and depth layers into a 64x64x3 image, with scalar task and gripper states encoded into image patches.
legacy_cells.AZ: Explicit finite-state-machine task-level states (successful termination, failed termination, normal progress, abnormal progress), tracked target and gripper masks.
legacy_cells.BD: Nine discrete commands per timestep, Cartesian translation in 2 mm increments, rotation in 10-degree increments about z, gripper open/closed.
legacy_cells.BH: Discrete policy commands directly actuate the robot gripper through the controller, evaluated in simulation and on a da Vinci PSM.
legacy_cells.BU: Sparse FSM-driven rewards: +1 successful grasp/lift termination, −0.1 failed termination at horizon, −0.001 normal progress, negative penalties for specified abnormal progress.
legacy_cells.BV: Maximize expected future discounted reward under the learned policy, with sparse FSM rewards and terminations.
legacy_cells.CK: Maximize expected future discounted reward, with discrete task rewards/penalties and a task horizon of 300 timesteps, desired gripper positions outside the workspace are clipped to the nearest point within it.
legacy_cells.DN: SurRoL simulation benchmark, da Vinci Surgical System / da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) robot experiments, Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera
legacy_cells.EC: Control/task success: simulation GAS success rate 87% with score 56 after 1.8 million training timesteps, real-robot aggregate success rate 69% with score 43 across the reported study, rectangle phantom 75%, liver phantom 70%.
legacy_cells.EG: Training used 1.8 million timesteps, each simulation experiment took 2–3 days, deployed real-robot controllers ran at around 2 Hz.
legacy_cells.EI: PPO (non-world-model baseline) did not learn successful grasping in simulation, the results narrative reports success below 1% for PPO.
legacy_cells.EJ: DreamerV2 world-model baseline did not learn successful grasping in simulation, the results narrative reports success below 1%.
legacy_cells.EK: GAS-RawVR (replace DSA with raw visual representation), GAS-NoDE (remove depth estimation), GAS-NoClutch (remove virtual clutch), GAS-NoDR (remove domain randomization).
legacy_cells.EL: Authors report failures when horizontal pushing moves the target outside the workspace, discrete small action increments limit gripper movement speed, FSM state identification relies on human observation/control.
legacy_cells.EM: Workspace boundary enforcement: desired gripper positions outside the workspace are clipped to the nearest point within the workspace.
legacy_cells.FL: Visual preprocessing: SAM/XMem-based masks, uncertainty-aware depth estimation, then DSA encodes mask/depth/global information and scalar states, DreamerV2 world model learns latent temporal dynamics and an imagined-rollout-trained visuomotor policy outputs discrete gripper commands, passed through a virtual clutch to the robot.
legacy_cells.FM: Authors contribute GAS for unified surgical grasping across diverse objects and grippers, empirical size-prior uncertainty-aware depth estimation, DSA visual representation, virtual clutch and domain randomization for stability/transfer, and FSM-based sparse rewards and terminations.
legacy_cells.FN: Reported simulation GAS success rate was 87% (score 56) after 1.8 million training timesteps. On real robots, aggregate success was 69% (score 43), the controller exceeded 75% success in five disturbance classes, and achieved 55% in re-grasping.
legacy_cells.FO: Authors state that failures occur when horizontal pushing moves the target outside the workspace, discrete incremental actions limit movement speed, and FSM-state identification depends on human observation and control.
legacy_cells.FP: Authors propose improving video object segmentation robustness, using continuous action spaces, reducing target sliding, extending GAS to tasks such as thread looping, and automating FSM-state identification.
legacy_cells.FQ: Authors identify difficulty applying world-model-based visuomotor learning to general surgical grasping because task objects are small relative to background, depth sensing is inaccurate, and millimeter-level control is required.
legacy_cells.FR: The reported evidence is technical grasping performance in simulation and phantom-based robot setups, not patient outcomes or clinical workflow benefit, the study does not establish prospective clinical readiness or causal treatment effects.
